paragraphs.sourceText: There are many understandable reasons why you might find it difficult to ask for help when you need it. Psychologists have been interested in this 1 for decades, not least because people’s widespread 2 to ask for help has led to some high-profile failures.
paragraphs.translationZh: 当您需要帮助时，您可能会发现很难寻求帮助，原因有很多可以理解的原因。几十年来，心理学家一直对这个问题感兴趣，尤其是因为人们普遍不愿寻求帮助，这导致了一些引人注目的失败。

paragraphs.sourceText: Asking for help takes 3 . It involves communicating a need on your part — there’s something you can’t do. 4 , you’re broadcasting your own weakness, which can be 5 . You might have 6 about losing control of whatever it is you are asking for help with. 7 someone starts to help, perhaps they will take over, or get a credit for your early efforts. Yet another 8 that you might be worried about is being a nuisance or 9 the person you go to for help.
paragraphs.translationZh: 寻求帮助需要勇气。它涉及到传达你的需求——有些事情你不能做。换句话说，你正在传播自己的弱点，这可能会让人感到不舒服。您可能会担心失去对您寻求帮助的内容的控制。一旦有人开始提供帮助，也许他们会接手，或者因为你早期的努力而得到认可。您可能担心的另一个因素是给您寻求帮助的人带来麻烦或不便。

paragraphs.sourceText: If you struggle with low self-esteem, you might find it especially difficult to 10 for help because you have the added worry of the other person 11 your request. You might see such refusals as implying something 12 about the status of your relationship with them. To 13 these difficulties, try to remind yourself that everyone needs help sometimes. Nobody knows everything and can do everything all by themselves. And while you might 14 coming across as incompetent, there’s actually research that shows that advice-seekers are 15 as more competent, not less.
paragraphs.translationZh: 如果您与低自尊作斗争，您可能会发现寻求帮助特别困难，因为您更担心对方拒绝您的请求。您可能会认为这种拒绝意味着您与他们的关系状况存在负面影响。为了克服这些困难，请尝试提醒自己每个人有时都需要帮助。没有人知道一切，也没有人能够独自完成一切。虽然你可能担心被认为是无能，但实际上有研究表明，寻求建议的人被认为更有能力，而不是更无能。

paragraphs.sourceText: Perhaps most encouraging of all is a paper from 2022 by researchers at Stanford University, in California, that involved a mix of contrived help-seeking interactions and asking people to 16 times they’d sought help in the past. The findings showed that help-seekers generally underestimate how 17 other people will be to help and how good it will make the help-giver feel (for most people, having the chance to help someone is highly 18 ).
paragraphs.translationZh: 也许最令人鼓舞的是加州斯坦福大学研究人员 2022 年发表的一篇论文，其中涉及人为的寻求帮助互动，并要求人们回忆过去寻求帮助的时间。研究结果表明，寻求帮助的人普遍低估了其他人提供帮助的意愿以及帮助者的感受有多好（对于大多数人来说，有机会帮助别人是非常有价值的）。

paragraphs.sourceText: So bear all this in mind the next time you need to ask for help. 19 , take care over who you ask and when you ask them. And if someone can’t help right now, avoid taking it personally. They might just be too 20 , or they might not feel confident about their ability to help.
paragraphs.translationZh: 因此，下次您需要寻求帮助时，请记住所有这些。另外，请注意你问的对象和时间。如果有人现在无法提供帮助，请避免将其视为针对个人。他们可能只是太忙了，或者他们可能对自己提供帮助的能力没有信心。

paragraphs.sourceText: U.S. customers historically tipped people they assumed were earning most of their income via tips, such as restaurant servers earning less than the minimum wage. In the early 2010s, a wide range of businesses started processing purchases with iPads and other digital payment systems. These systems often prompted customers to tip for services that were not previously tipped.
paragraphs.translationZh: 历史上，美国顾客向他们认为大部分收入来自小费的人支付小费，例如收入低于最低工资的餐馆服务员。 2010 年代初，许多企业开始使用 iPad 和其他数字支付系统处理购买行为。这些系统经常提示顾客为以前没有给过小费的服务支付小费。

paragraphs.sourceText: Today’s tip requests are often not connected to the salary and service norms that used to determine when and how people tip. Customers in the past nearly always paid tips after receiving a service, such as at the conclusion of a restaurant meal, after getting a haircut or once a pizza was delivered. That timing could reward high-quality service and give workers an incentive to provide it.
paragraphs.translationZh: 如今的小费请求通常与用于确定人们何时以及如何给小费的工资和服务规范无关。过去，顾客几乎总是在接受服务后支付小费，例如在餐厅用餐结束时、理发后或披萨送达后。这个时机可以奖励高质量的服务，并激励员工提供服务。

paragraphs.sourceText: It’s becoming more common for tips to be requested beforehand. And new tipping technology may even automatically add tips.
paragraphs.translationZh: 提前索取小费的情况变得越来越普遍。新的小费技术甚至可以自动添加小费。

paragraphs.sourceText: The prevalence of digital payment devices has made it easier to ask customers for a tip. That helps explain why tip requests are creeping into new kinds of services. Customers now routinely see menus of suggested default options — often well above 20% of what they owe. The amounts have risen from 10% or less in the 1950s to 15% around the year 2000 to 20% or higher today. This increase is sometimes called tipflation — the expectation of ever-higher tip amounts.
paragraphs.translationZh: 数字支付设备的普及使得向顾客索要小费变得更加容易。这有助于解释为什么小费请求正在渗透到新型服务中。现在，客户经常会看到建议的默认选项菜单——通常远高于他们所欠金额的 20%。这一数字已从 2000 年左右的 1950 年代的 10% 或更少上升到 15%，再到今天的 20% 或更高。这种增加有时被称为小费膨胀——小费金额越来越高的预期。

paragraphs.sourceText: Tipping has always been a vital source of income for workers in historically tipped services, like restaurants, where the tipped minimum wage can be as low as US $2.13 an hour. Tip creep and tipflation are now further supplementing the income of many low-wage service workers.
paragraphs.translationZh: 对于历史上需要小费的服务业（例如餐馆）的工人来说，小费一直是重要的收入来源，这些服务业的小费最低工资可低至每小时 2.13 美元。小费攀升和小费膨胀现在进一步补充了许多低薪服务业工人的收入。

paragraphs.sourceText: Notably, tipping primarily benefits some of these workers, such as waiters, but not others, such as cooks and dishwashers. To ensure that all employees were paid fair wages, some restaurants banned tipping and increased prices, but this movement towards no-tipping services has largely fizzled out.
paragraphs.translationZh: 值得注意的是，小费主要有利于其中一些工人，例如服务员，但不适用于其他工人，例如厨师和洗碗工。为了确保所有员工得到公平的工资，一些餐馆禁止给小费并提高价格，但这种不给小费服务的运动基本上以失败告终。

paragraphs.sourceText: So to increase employee wages without raising prices, more employers are succumbing to temptations of tip creep and tipflation. However, many customers are frustrated because they feel they are being asked for too high of a tip too often. And, as our research emphasizes, tipping now seems to be more coercive, less generous, and often completely dissociated from service quality.
paragraphs.translationZh: 因此，为了在不提高物价的情况下提高员工工资，越来越多的雇主屈服于小费攀升和小费膨胀的诱惑。然而，许多顾客感到沮丧，因为他们觉得自己经常被要求支付过高的小费。而且，正如我们的研究所强调的那样，现在的小费似乎更具强制性，不那么慷慨，而且往往与服务质量完全无关。

paragraphs.sourceText: When it was established, the National Health Service (NHS) was visionary: offering high-quality, timely care to meet the dominant needs of the population it served. Nearly 75 years on, with the UK facing very different health challenges, it is clear that the model is out of date.
paragraphs.translationZh: 国家医疗服务体系 (NHS) 成立之初就抱有远见：提供高质量、及时的护理，以满足其所服务人群的主要需求。近 75 年过去了，英国面临着截然不同的健康挑战，显然该模型已经过时了。

paragraphs.sourceText: From life expectancy to cancer and infant mortality rates, we are lagging behind many of our peers. With more than 6.8 million on waitlists, healthcare is becoming increasingly inaccessible for those who cannot opt to pay for private treatment; and the cost of providing healthcare is increasingly squeezing our investment in other public services. As demand for healthcare continues to grow, pressures on the workforce — which is already near breaking point — will only become more acute.
paragraphs.translationZh: 从预期寿命到癌症和婴儿死亡率，我们落后于许多同龄人。等候名单上有超过 680 万人，对于那些无法选择支付私人治疗费用的人来说，医疗保健变得越来越困难；提供医疗保健的成本日益挤压我们对其他公共服务的投资。随着医疗保健需求持续增长，劳动力面临的压力（已经接近临界点）只会变得更加严峻。

paragraphs.sourceText: Many of the answers to the crisis in health and care are well rehearsed. We need to be much better at reducing and diverting demand on health services, rather than simply managing it. Much more needs to be invested in communities and primary care to reduce our reliance on hospitals. And capacity in social care needs to be greater, to support the growing number of people living with long-term conditions.
paragraphs.translationZh: 针对健康和护理危机的许多答案都是经过精心设计的。我们需要更好地减少和转移对卫生服务的需求，而不是简单地对其进行管理。需要对社区和初级保健进行更多投资，以减少我们对医院的依赖。社会护理能力需要更大，以支持越来越多的长期患有疾病的人。

paragraphs.sourceText: Yet despite two decades of strategies and a number of major health reforms, we have failed to make meaningful progress on any of these aims. That is why the Reform think tank is launching a new programme of work entitled “Reimagining health”, supported by ten former health ministers. Together, we are calling for a much more open and honest conversation about the future of health in the UK, and an “urgent rethink” of the hospital-centric model we retain.
paragraphs.translationZh: 然而，尽管制定了二十年的战略并进行了一系列重大的卫生改革，我们仍未能在这些目标上取得有意义的进展。这就是为什么改革智囊团正在启动一项题为“重新构想健康”的新工作计划，并得到了十位前卫生部长的支持。我们共同呼吁就英国健康的未来进行更加公开和诚实的对话，并“紧急重新思考”我们保留的以医院为中心的模式。

paragraphs.sourceText: This must begin with the question of how we maximise the health of the nation, rather than “fix” the NHS. It is estimated, for example, that healthcare accounts for only about 20% of health outcomes. Much more important are the places we live, work and socialise — yet there is no clear cross-government strategy for improving these social determinants of health. Worse, when policies like the national obesity strategy are scrapped, taxpayers are left with the hefty price tag of treating the illnesses, like diabetes, that result.
paragraphs.translationZh: 这必须从如何最大限度地提高国民健康水平开始，而不是“修复”国民医疗服务体系。例如，据估计，医疗保健仅占健康结果的 20% 左右。更重要的是我们生活、工作和社交的地方——但目前还没有明确的跨政府战略来改善这些健康的社会决定因素。更糟糕的是，当国家肥胖战略等政策被废除时，纳税人将承担治疗糖尿病等疾病的高昂费用。

paragraphs.sourceText: Reform wants to ask how power and resources should be distributed in our health system. What health functions should remain at the centre, and what should be given to local leaders, often responsible for services that create health, and with a much better understanding of the needs of their populations?
paragraphs.translationZh: 改革想问的是我们的卫生系统中的权力和资源应该如何分配。哪些卫生职能应保留在中心位置，哪些应交给地方领导人，他们通常负责创造健康的服务，并更好地了解其人民的需求？

paragraphs.sourceText: Heat action plans, or HAPs, have been proliferating in India in the past few years. In general, an HAP spells out when and how officials should issue heat warnings and alert hospitals and other institutions. Nagpur’s plan, for instance, calls for hospitals to set aside “cold wards” in the summer for treating heatstroke patients, and advises builders to give construction laborers a break from work on very hot days.
paragraphs.translationZh: 过去几年，印度的高温行动计划（HAP）不断增多。一般来说，HAP 详细说明了官员应何时以及如何发布高温警报并向医院和其他机构发出警报。例如，那格浦尔的计划要求医院在夏季设立“冷病房”来治疗中暑患者，并建议建筑商在炎热的日子里让建筑工人休息一下。

paragraphs.sourceText: But implementation of existing HAPs has been uneven, according to a report from the center for Policy Research. Many lack adequate funding, it found. And their triggering thresholds often are not customized to the local climate. In some areas, high daytime temperatures alone might serve as an adequate trigger for alerts. But in other places, nighttime temperatures or humidity might be as important a gauge of risk as daytime highs.
paragraphs.translationZh: 但根据政策研究中心的一份报告，现有 HAP 的实施情况并不均衡。报告发现，许多人缺乏足够的资金。而且它们的触发阈值通常不是根据当地气候定制的。在某些地区，仅白天高温就足以触发警报。但在其他地方，夜间温度或湿度可能与白天的最高温度一样重要。

paragraphs.sourceText: Mumbai’s April heat stroke deaths highlighted the need for more nuanced and localized warnings, researchers say. That day’s high temperature of roughly 36°C was 1°C shy of the heat wave alert threshold for coastal cities set by national meteorological authorities. But the effects of the heat were amplified by humidity — an often neglected factor in heat alert systems — and the lack of shade at the late-morning outdoor ceremony.
paragraphs.translationZh: 研究人员表示，孟买四月份的中暑死亡事件凸显了需要采取更细致、更局部的警告。当日最高气温约36℃，较国家气象部门设定的沿海城市热浪警报阈值低1℃。但湿度（高温警报系统中经常被忽视的一个因素）以及上午晚些时候的户外仪式缺乏遮荫，加剧了高温的影响。

paragraphs.sourceText: To help improve HAPs, urban planner Kotharkar’s team is working on a model plan that outlines best practices and could be adapted to local conditions. Among other things, she says, all cities should create a vulnerability map to help focus responses on the populations most at risk.
paragraphs.translationZh: 为了帮助改善 HAP，城市规划师 Kotharkar 的团队正在制定一个模型计划，该计划概述了最佳实践，并且可以根据当地情况进行调整。她说，除其他外，所有城市都应该创建一个脆弱性地图，以帮助将应对措施集中在最危险的人群上。

paragraphs.sourceText: Such mapping doesn’t need to be complex, Kotharkar says. “A useful map can be created by looking at even a few key parameters.” For example, neighborhoods with a large elderly population or informal dwellings that cope poorly with heat could get special warnings or be bolstered with cooling centers. The Nagpur project has already created a risk and vulnerability map, which enabled Kotharkar to tell officials which neighborhoods to focus on in the event of a heat wave this summer.
paragraphs.translationZh: 科塔卡说，这种映射不需要很复杂。 “甚至可以通过查看几个关键参数来创建有用的地图。”例如，老年人口较多的社区或应对炎热天气不佳的非正式住宅可能会收到特别警告或得到降温中心的支持。那格浦尔项目已经创建了风险和脆弱性地图，这使得科塔卡能够告诉官员在今年夏天发生热浪时应该关注哪些社区。

paragraphs.sourceText: HAPs shouldn’t just include short-term emergency responses, researchers say, but also recommend medium- to long-term measures that could make communities cooler. In Nagpur, for example, Kotharkar’s team has been able to advise city officials about where to plant trees to provide shade. HAPs could also guide efforts to retrofit homes or modify building regulations. “Reducing deaths in an emergency is a good target to have, but it’s the lowest target,” says Climate researcher Chandni Singh.
paragraphs.translationZh: 研究人员表示，HAP 不应只包括短期应急响应，还应建议采取中长期措施，使社区降温。例如，在那格浦尔，科塔卡的团队已经能够向市政府官员提供有关在哪里种植树木以提供遮荫的建议。 HAP 还可以指导房屋改造或修改建筑法规的工作。 “减少紧急情况下的死亡人数是一个很好的目标，但这是最低的目标，”气候研究员钱德尼·辛格说。

paragraphs.sourceText: Navigating beyond the organised pavements and parks of our urban spaces, desire paths are the unofficial footprints of a community, revealing the unspoken preferences, shared shortcuts and collective choices of humans. Often appearing as trodden dirt tracks through otherwise neat green spaces, these routes of collective disobedience cut corners, bisect lawns and cross hills, representing the natural capability of people (and animals) to go from point A to point B most effectively.
paragraphs.translationZh: 欲望路径超越了我们城市空间的有组织的人行道和公园，是一个社区的非官方足迹，揭示了人类不言而喻的偏好、共享的捷径和集体选择。这些集体抗命路线通常表现为穿过原本整洁的绿地的土路，它们抄近路、一分为二、穿过山丘，代表了人（和动物）最有效地从 A 点到 B 点的自然能力。

paragraphs.sourceText: Urban planners interpret desire paths as more than just convenient shortcuts; they offer valuable insights into the dynamics between planning and behaviour. Ohio State University allowed its students to navigate the Oval, a lawn in the centre of campus, freely, then proceeded to pave the desire paths, creating a web of effective routes students had established.
paragraphs.translationZh: 城市规划者将欲望路径解释为不仅仅是方便的捷径；它们为规划和行为之间的动态提供了宝贵的见解。俄亥俄州立大学允许学生自由地在校园中心的草坪——椭圆形草坪上行走，然后开始铺设理想的道路，创建学生们建立的有效路线网。

paragraphs.sourceText: Yet, reluctance persists among other planners to integrate desire paths into formal plans, citing concerns about safety, environmental impact, or primarily, aesthetics. A Reddit webpage devoted to the phenomenon, boasting nearly 50,000 members, showcases images of local desire paths adorned with signs instructing pedestrians to adhere to designated walkways, underscoring the rebellious nature inherent in these human-made tracks. This clash highlights an ongoing struggle between the organic, user-driven evolution of public spaces and the desire for a visually curated and controlled urban environment.
paragraphs.translationZh: 然而，其他规划者仍然不愿将愿望路径纳入正式规划，理由是担心安全、环境影响或主要是美观。 Reddit 的一个致力于这一现象的网页拥有近 50,000 名会员，展示了当地欲望之路的图像，上面装饰着指示行人遵守指定人行道的标志，强调了这些人造轨道固有的叛逆本质。这种冲突凸显了公共空间的有机、用户驱动的演变与对视觉策划和控制的城市环境的渴望之间持续存在的斗争。

paragraphs.sourceText: The Wickquasgeck Trail is an example of a historical desire path, created by Native Americans to cross the forests of Manhattan and move between settlements quickly. This trail, when Dutch colonists arrived, was widened and made into one of the main trade roads across the island, known at the time as de Heere Straat, or Gentlemen’s Street. Following the British assumption of control in New York, the street was renamed Broadway. Notably, Broadway stands out as one of the few areas in NYC that defies the grid-based system applied to the rest of the city, cutting a diagonal across parts of the city.
paragraphs.translationZh: 威克夸斯盖克步道 (Wickquasgeck Trail) 是历史上渴望之路的一个例子，由美洲原住民创建，用于穿越曼哈顿的森林并在定居点之间快速移动。当荷兰殖民者到达时，这条小路被拓宽，成为横贯该岛的主要贸易道路之一，当时被称为德希尔海峡或绅士街。英国控制纽约后，这条街更名为百老汇。值得注意的是，百老汇是纽约市少数几个不遵守应用于城市其他地区的基于网格的系统的地区之一，在城市的部分地区划出了一条对角线。

paragraphs.sourceText: In online spaces, desire paths have sparked a fascination that can approach obsession, with the Reddit page serving as a hub. Contributors offer a wide array of stories, from little-known new shortcuts to long-established alternate routes.
paragraphs.translationZh: 在网络空间中，以 Reddit 页面为中心，欲望路径引发了一种近乎痴迷的迷恋。贡献者提供了各种各样的故事，从鲜为人知的新捷径到历史悠久的替代路线。

paragraphs.sourceText: Animal desire paths, such as ducks forging trails through frozen ponds or dogs carving direct routes in gardens, highlight the adaptability of these trails in both human and animal experiences. As desire paths criss-cross through both physical and virtual landscapes, they stand as a proof of the collective insistence on forging unconventional routes and embracing the spirit of communal choice.
paragraphs.translationZh: 动物渴望的路径，例如鸭子在结冰的池塘中开辟出的路径或狗在花园中开辟出的直接路径，突显了这些路径在人类和动物体验中的适应性。当欲望路径在物理和虚拟景观中纵横交错时，它们证明了集体坚持开辟非传统路线和拥抱公共选择精神。

paragraphs.sourceText: Read the following text and answer the questions by choosing the most suitable subheading from the list A-G for each of the numbered paragraphs (41-45). There are two extra subheadings which you do not need to use. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)
paragraphs.translationZh: 阅读以下文字并从 A-G 列表中为每个编号段落 (41-45) 选择最合适的副标题来回答问题。有两个额外的副标题您不需要使用。在答题卡上标记您的答案。 （10分）

paragraphs.sourceText: Five Steps to Suggesting a Change at Work That’ll Actually Get Taken Seriously
paragraphs.translationZh: 建议工作改变的五个步骤实际上会得到认真对待

paragraphs.sourceText: Everyone wants to be that person — the one who looks at the same information as everyone else, but who sees a fresh, innovative solution. However, it takes more than simply having a good idea. How you share it is as important as the suggestion itself.
paragraphs.translationZh: 每个人都想成为这样的人——与其他人看到相同的信息，但看到新鲜、创新的解决方案的人。然而，仅仅有一个好主意是不够的。如何分享它与建议本身一样重要。

paragraphs.sourceText: Why? Because writing a new script — literally or figuratively — means that other team members will have to adapt to something new. So whether you’re suggesting a (seemingly) benign change like streamlining outdated protocol, or a bigger change like adding an hour to each workday so people can leave early on Fridays, you’re asking others to reimagine their workflow or schedule. Not to mention, if the process you’re scrapping is one someone else suggested, there’s the possibility of hurt feelings.
paragraphs.translationZh: 为什么？因为编写新剧本——无论是字面意思还是象征意义——都意味着其他团队成员将不得不适应新的东西。因此，无论您是建议进行（看似）良性的改变（例如简化过时的协议），还是进行更大的更改（例如每个工作日增加一个小时以便人们可以在周五提前下班），您都是在要求其他人重新构想他们的工作流程或时间表。更不用说，如果你要放弃的流程是别人建议的，则可能会伤害感情。

paragraphs.sourceText: To gain buy-in on an innovative, new idea, follow these steps:
paragraphs.translationZh: 要获得创新的新想法的支持，请按照以下步骤操作：

paragraphs.sourceText: Great ideas don’t stand alone. In other words, you can’t mention your suggestion once and expect it to be adopted. To see a change, you’ll need to champion your plan and sell its merits. In addition, you need to be willing to stand up to scrutiny and criticism and be prepared to explain your innovation in different ways for various audiences.
paragraphs.translationZh: 伟大的想法并不是孤立的。换句话说，你不能提出你的建议一次就指望它被采纳。要看到改变，您需要支持您的计划并宣传其优点。此外，您需要愿意经受住审查和批评，并准备好以不同的方式向不同的受众解释您的创新。

paragraphs.sourceText: Sometimes it makes sense to go to your boss first. But other times, it’s useful to build a coalition among your co-workers or other stakeholders. When it works, it works great — because you’re ready for your stubborn supervisor’s pushback with answers like, “Actually, I connected with a few people in our tech department to discuss how much time these kinds of website updates would take, and they suggested they have the bandwidth.”
paragraphs.translationZh: 有时先去找你的老板是有意义的。但其他时候，在同事或其他利益相关者之间建立联盟很有用。当它起作用时，它效果很好——因为你已经准备好接受顽固的主管的抵制，并给出这样的答案：“实际上，我与我们技术部门的一些人联系，讨论此类网站更新需要多长时间，他们建议他们有足够的带宽。”

paragraphs.sourceText: One of the biggest barriers to gaining buy-in occurs when the owner of an idea is viewed as argumentative, defensive, or close-minded. Because, let’s be honest: No one likes a know-it-all. So, if people disagree with you, don’t be indignant. Instead, listen to their concerns fully, try to understand their perspective, and include their concerns (and possible remedies) in future discussions.
paragraphs.translationZh: 当一个想法的所有者被视为好争论、防御性或思想封闭时，获得认同的最大障碍之一就会出现。因为，说实话：没有人喜欢万事通。所以，如果有人不同意你的观点，不要愤怒。相反，充分倾听他们的担忧，尝试理解他们的观点，并将他们的担忧（以及可能的补救措施）纳入未来的讨论中。

paragraphs.sourceText: So, instead of saying, “Martha, our current slogan is confusing and should be updated,” you could try, “Martha raises a great point that our current slogan has a long history for our stakeholders, but I wonder if we might be able to brainstorm a tagline that could build on that — and be clearer for new customers.”
paragraphs.translationZh: 因此，你不要说“玛莎，我们当前的口号令人困惑，应该更新”，你可以尝试，“玛莎提出了一个很好的观点，即我们当前的口号对我们的利益相关者来说有着悠久的历史，但我想知道我们是否能够集思广益，提出一个可以以此为基础的口号，并且对新客户来说更清晰。”

paragraphs.sourceText: New ideas are the grandchildren of old ones. In other words, don’t throw old solutions under the bus to make your improvement stand out. Remember that in light of whatever the problem the old system solved — or, maybe, has failed to solve in recent memory — it was a great idea at the time. Appreciating the older contributions as you suggest future innovations helps bolster the credibility of your idea.
paragraphs.translationZh: 新想法是旧想法的孙子。换句话说，不要为了让你的改进脱颖而出而抛弃旧的解决方案。请记住，无论旧系统解决了什么问题——或者，也许在最近的记忆中未能解决——这在当时都是一个好主意。在建议未来创新时欣赏旧的贡献有助于增强您想法的可信度。

paragraphs.sourceText: When pitching a new idea, it’s important to use the language of abundance instead of the language of deficit. Instead of saying what is wrong, broken, or suboptimal, talk about what is right, fixable, or ideal. For example, try, “I can see lots of applications for this new approach” rather than, “This innovation is the only way.” Be optimistic but realistic, and you will stand out.
paragraphs.translationZh: 在提出新想法时，重要的是使用丰富的语言而不是赤字的语言。不要说什么是错的、坏的或次优的，而要谈论什么是正确的、可修复的或理想的。例如，尝试“我可以看到这种新方法的很多应用”，而不是“这种创新是唯一的方法”。乐观但现实，你就会脱颖而出。

paragraphs.sourceText: Translate the following text into Chinese. Write your translation on the ANSWER SHEET. (15 points)
paragraphs.translationZh: 将下列文字翻译成中文。将您的翻译写在答题卡上。 （15分）

paragraphs.sourceText: You know the moment — the conversation slows, then there’s a pause. It’s awkward, and so awkward that some people will panic and say anything. Do we all find such silences so stressful?
paragraphs.translationZh: 你知道那一刻——谈话变慢，然后停顿。这很尴尬，尴尬到有些人会惊慌失措，说什么都说不出来。我们都觉得这样的沉默很有压力吗？

paragraphs.sourceText: Researchers analysed the frequency and impact of gaps greater than 2 seconds during conversations, including an overview of previous studies which indicate that the fear of awkward silences can be so extreme that people avoid talking to strangers, even though doing so is likely to be an enjoyable experience.
paragraphs.translationZh: 研究人员分析了对话期间超过 2 秒的间隙的频率和影响，包括对先前研究的概述，这些研究表明，对尴尬的沉默的恐惧可能非常严重，以至于人们会避免与陌生人交谈，尽管这样做可能是一种愉快的经历。

paragraphs.sourceText: During conversations with short gaps, people feel more connected to their conversation partners. But such feelings of connection markedly dip when entering a long gap. Long gaps between strangers are likely to be followed by a change in topic.
paragraphs.translationZh: 在间隙较短的对话中，人们会感觉与对话伙伴的联系更加紧密。但当进入一段较长的间隙时，这种联系感就会明显下降。陌生人之间长时间的间隔很可能会改变话题。

paragraphs.sourceText: But the opposite seems to be true for conversations between friends. Long gaps there saw increased connection. Between friends, longer gaps seem to provide natural moments for reflection and expression.
paragraphs.translationZh: 但朋友之间的对话似乎恰恰相反。那里的长距离增加了联系。朋友之间，较长的间隔似乎为反思和表达提供了自然的时刻。
